claim: Antalarmin completely abolished sociability deficits induced by morphine in male C57BL/6J mice.
source: Antalarmin completely abolished sociability deficits induced by morphine in male, but not in female, C57BL/6J mice.
evidence: The manuscript reports behavioral data from the three-chamber test showing that antalarmin/morphine-treated male mice spent more time with the unfamiliar conspecific than with the object (p < 0.005) and showed higher sociability ratio than vehicle/morphine-treated mice (p < 0.005).

claim: Antalarmin did not abolish sociability deficits induced by morphine in female C57BL/6J mice.
source: Antalarmin completely abolished sociability deficits induced by morphine in male, but not in female, C57BL/6J mice.
evidence: The manuscript reports that morphine-treated female mice spent similar time in the ROIs containing the unfamiliar conspecific or the object (p = 0.259), independently of vehicle or antalarmin pretreatment, and showed lower sociability ratio than saline-treated mice (p < 0.05), independently of vehicle or antalarmin pretreatment.

claim: Genetic CRF1 receptor-deficiency eliminated morphine-induced sociability deficits in male mice.
source: Accordingly, genetic CRF1 receptor-deficiency eliminated morphine-induced sociability deficits in male mice.
evidence: The manuscript reports that morphine-treated CRF1 KO mice spent more time with the conspecific than with the object (p < 0.005), did not differ from saline-treated mice (p = 0.819) and showed higher sociability ratio than morphine-treated CRF1 WT and CRF1 HET mice (p < 0.05).

claim: Antalarmin eliminated morphine-induced firing of PVN neurons in male C57BL/6J mice.
source: Ex vivo electrophysiology studies showed that antalarmin also eliminated morphine-induced firing of PVN neurons in male, but not in female, C57BL/6J mice.
evidence: The manuscript reports that vehicle/morphine-treated male mice showed higher firing frequency than vehicle/saline-treated mice (p < 0.0005), while antalarmin/morphine-treated mice did not differ from saline-treated mice (p = 0.552) and showed lower firing frequency than vehicle/morphine-treated mice (p < 0.005).

claim: Antalarmin did not eliminate morphine-induced firing of PVN neurons in female C57BL/6J mice.
source: Ex vivo electrophysiology studies showed that antalarmin also eliminated morphine-induced firing of PVN neurons in male, but not in female, C57BL/6J mice.
evidence: The manuscript reports that in female mice, morphine similarly increased firing frequency in vehicle- or antalarmin-pretreated mice, as compared to saline-treated mice (p < 0.0005), with no pretreatment × treatment interaction effect.

claim: Genetic CRF1 receptor-deficiency reduced morphine-induced firing of PVN neurons in a CRF1 gene expression-dependent manner.
source: Likewise, genetic CRF1 receptor-deficiency reduced morphine-induced firing of PVN neurons in a CRF1 gene expression-dependent manner.
evidence: The manuscript reports that morphine increased firing frequency in CRF1 WT (p < 0.0005) and in CRF1 HET (p < 0.005), but not in CRF1 KO (p = 0.987), mice, and that morphine-treated CRF1 HET mice showed lower or higher firing frequency than morphine-treated CRF1 WT (p < 0.05) or CRF1 KO (p < 0.005) mice, respectively.

claim: The electrophysiology results consistently mirrored the behavioral results, indicating a link between morphine-induced PVN activity and sociability deficits.
source: The electrophysiology results consistently mirrored the behavioral results, indicating a link between morphine-induced PVN activity and sociability deficits.
evidence: The manuscript reports parallel effects of antalarmin and CRF1 receptor-deficiency on both sociability deficits and PVN neuronal firing in male mice.

claim: In male mice, antalarmin abolished morphine-induced firing in neurons co-expressing OXY and AVP.
source: Interestingly, in male mice antalarmin abolished morphine-induced firing in neurons co-expressing OXY and AVP, but not in neurons expressing only AVP.
evidence: The manuscript reports that vehicle/morphine-treated male mice showed higher firing frequency of OXY/AVP-expressing neurons than vehicle/saline-treated mice (p < 0.0005), while antalarmin/morphine-treated mice did not differ from saline-treated mice (p = 0.782) and showed lower firing frequency than vehicle/morphine-treated mice (p < 0.0005).

claim: In male mice, antalarmin did not abolish morphine-induced firing in neurons expressing only AVP.
source: Interestingly, in male mice antalarmin abolished morphine-induced firing in neurons co-expressing OXY and AVP, but not in neurons expressing only AVP.
evidence: The manuscript reports that morphine increased firing frequency of neurons expressing AVP, but not OXY, independently of vehicle or antalarmin pretreatment (p < 0.05).

claim: In female mice, antalarmin did not affect morphine-induced firing of neurons co-expressing OXY and AVP.
source: In contrast, in female mice antalarmin did not affect morphine-induced firing of neurons co-expressing OXY and AVP or only OXY, indicating a selective sex-specific role for the CRF1 receptor in opiate-induced PVN OXY activity.
evidence: The manuscript reports that in female mice, morphine increased firing frequency of neurons co-expressing OXY and AVP, independently of vehicle or antalarmin pretreatment (p < 0.005).

claim: In female mice, antalarmin did not affect morphine-induced firing of neurons expressing only OXY.
source: In contrast, in female mice antalarmin did not affect morphine-induced firing of neurons co-expressing OXY and AVP or only OXY, indicating a selective sex-specific role for the CRF1 receptor in opiate-induced PVN OXY activity.
evidence: The manuscript reports that in female mice, morphine increased firing frequency of neurons expressing OXY, but not AVP, independently of vehicle or antalarmin pretreatment (p < 0.005).

claim: There is a selective sex-specific role for the CRF1 receptor in opiate-induced PVN OXY activity.
source: In contrast, in female mice antalarmin did not affect morphine-induced firing of neurons co-expressing OXY and AVP or only OXY, indicating a selective sex-specific role for the CRF1 receptor in opiate-induced PVN OXY activity.
evidence: The manuscript reports differential effects of antalarmin on morphine-induced firing of OXY-expressing neurons between male and female mice.

claim: The present findings demonstrate a major, sex-linked, role for the CRF1 receptor in sociability deficits and related brain alterations induced by morphine.
source: The present findings demonstrate a major, sex-linked, role for the CRF1 receptor in sociability deficits and related brain alterations induced by morphine, suggesting new therapeutic strategy for opiate use disorders.
evidence: The manuscript reports that both pharmacological and genetic disruption of CRF1 receptor function eliminated morphine-induced sociability deficits and PVN neuronal firing in male, but not in female, mice.

claim: The findings suggest a new therapeutic strategy for opiate use disorders.
source: The present findings demonstrate a major, sex-linked, role for the CRF1 receptor in sociability deficits and related brain alterations induced by morphine, suggesting new therapeutic strategy for opiate use disorders.
evidence: The manuscript demonstrates that CRF1 receptor antagonism eliminates morphine-induced sociability deficits in male mice.

claim: Opiate substances often induce severe social behavior deficits, such as poor sociability, social isolation, and elevated aggressiveness.
source: Opiate substances often induce severe social behavior deficits, such as poor sociability, social isolation, and elevated aggressiveness (Babor et al., 1976; Gerra et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

source: Notably, opiate-induced social behavior deficits dramatically contribute to addictive-like substance consumption, favoring the development and maintenance of opiate use disorders (OUD) (APA, 2013; Pomrenze et al., 2022).

claim: Chemogenetic inhibition of OXY-expressing neurons within the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus decreased social approach in male mice.
